exercises.title: A radius in two norms
exercises.q: A logit map with input domain $\mathbb R^3$ has certified Euclidean Lipschitz bound $L=2$ and positive margin $m=0.6$. Compute the strict Euclidean robustness radius and a sufficient $\ell_\infty$ radius. Does equality at either radius certify the label?
exercises.hint: First divide by $\sqrt2L$, then use $\|\delta\|_2\le\sqrt3\|\delta\|_\infty$.
steps: The difference of two logits has Lipschitz bound $\sqrt2L$, so the margin stays positive whenever $0.6-2\sqrt2\|\delta\|_2\gt0$. Solving gives $r_2=0.6/(2\sqrt2)\approx0.212132$.
An infinity-norm perturbation of size $r_\infty$ can have Euclidean norm $\sqrt3r_\infty$. Thus $r_\infty=r_2/\sqrt3=0.6/(2\sqrt6)\approx0.122474$ is sufficient, with a strict inequality.
At equality the lower bound on a margin is zero. A tie may change the label, so these rules certify open balls unless a suitable tie convention is separately justified.

exercises.title: Which direction does a product bound pay for?
exercises.q: Let $W_0=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)$ and $W_1=[0\ \ 2]$, with zero biases and ReLU between them. Compute the product bound and the exact Lipschitz constant of $f(x)=W_1\operatorname{ReLU}(W_0x)$.
exercises.hint: Write the scalar output explicitly before multiplying norms.
steps: The largest singular value of $W_0$ is $3$, and the Euclidean norm of the row $W_1$ is $2$. The product bound is therefore $6$.
The first hidden coordinate is multiplied by zero at the output. Consequently $f(x)=2\operatorname{ReLU}(x_2)$, whose slope in the second coordinate is either $0$ or $2$.

ReLU is 1-Lipschitz, so $|f(x)-f(y)|\le2|x_2-y_2|\le2\|x-y\|_2$. Equality occurs for two distinct inputs with positive second coordinate and equal first coordinate. Thus $L^\star=2$; the product paid for an unused direction.

exercises.title: Read a scalar quadratic constraint
exercises.q: For slope bounds $[0,1]$, evaluate $q(u,w)=2w(u-w)$ at $(u,w)=(2,1),(2,3),(2,-1)$. Which pairs could be increments of a slope-restricted function?
exercises.hint: For $u\ne0$, the chord slope is $w/u$.
steps: The first pair has slope $1/2$, which belongs to $[0,1]$. The other slopes are $3/2$ and $-1/2$, which violate the upper bound and monotonicity respectively.
For a single increment pair the nonnegative QC is equivalent to the allowed slope interval. It does not determine which activation or basepoints produced the pair.

exercises.title: The bound or its square?
exercises.q: A valid LipSDP certificate returns $\rho=9/4$. What bound does it certify? A sampled gradient has norm $1.6$. Can both computations be correct for this same network and norm?
exercises.hint: The performance inequality compares squared norms.
steps: LipSDP proves $\|\Delta f\|^2\le\rho\|\Delta x\|^2$. Taking nonnegative square roots gives $L=\sqrt{9/4}=3/2=1.5$.
At a differentiability point a gradient or Jacobian norm of $1.6$ gives the lower bound $L^\star\ge1.6$. The certificate would give $L^\star\le1.5$.

These statements contradict each other. Recheck the matrix feasibility, the multiplier assumptions, the gradient calculation, preprocessing and the norm convention. Sampling alone cannot validate an upper bound, but it can refute one.

exercises.title: A complete scalar LipSDP certificate
exercises.q: For $f(x)=2\operatorname{ReLU}(3x+b)$, substitute $T=4$ and $\rho=36$ in the one-hidden-layer LMI. Factor the resulting matrix to prove feasibility. Is the bound tight for any finite $b$?
exercises.hint: For $[0,1]$ slopes, the matrix is $[ -\rho,\ 3T;\ 3T,\ -2T+4]$.
steps: Substitution gives $M=\begin{bmatrix}-36&12\\12&-4\end{bmatrix}=-4\begin{bmatrix}3\\-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\end{bmatrix}$.
For every vector $\xi$, $\xi^\top M\xi=-4(3\xi_1-\xi_2)^2\le0$. Also $T=4\ge0$, so all certificate conditions hold and $L\le\sqrt{36}=6$.
When $x\gt-b/3$, the neuron is active and $f(x)=6x+2b$. Two distinct inputs in this half-line attain difference ratio $6$. Hence $L^\star=6$ for every finite bias.

exercises.title: Add neuron constraints with valid weights
exercises.q: Take $u=(2,-2)$, $w=(1,-1/2)$ and diagonal $T=\operatorname{diag}(3,2)$. Evaluate $2w^\top T(u-w)$. Explain why allowing a negative diagonal entry would invalidate the general argument.
exercises.hint: Evaluate one channel at a time; nonnegative sums preserve inequalities.
steps: The channel contributions are $2\cdot3\cdot1\cdot(2-1)=6$ and $2\cdot2\cdot(-1/2)\cdot(-2+1/2)=3$, so the total is $9$.
The slopes are $1/2$ and $1/4$, both in $[0,1]$. Each unweighted scalar QC is nonnegative; multiplying by $3$ and $2$ and summing preserves that sign.

A negative multiplier reverses the inequality for a channel. For instance the first channel alone with weight $-1$ gives $-2$. Diagonal structure supplies valid individual constraints, and nonnegative weights preserve them.

exercises.title: A loop transformation can see cancellation
exercises.q: Let $W_0=[1\ \ -1]^\top$, $W_1=[1\ \ 1]$ and $f(x)=W_1\operatorname{ReLU}(W_0x)$. Compare the product bound with $U=\tfrac12\|W_1W_0\|+\tfrac12\|W_1\|\|W_0\|$. Find the exact constant.
exercises.hint: Use $\operatorname{ReLU}(x)+\operatorname{ReLU}(-x)=|x|$.
steps: Both weight norms equal $\sqrt2$, so the product is $2$. But $W_1W_0=1-1=0$, giving $U=0+\tfrac12\cdot2=1$.
The loop transformation writes ReLU as $t/2+r(t)$ with $r$ having slopes in $[-1/2,1/2]$. The linear term cancels in this network; only the half-Lipschitz remainder contributes.
The actual output is $|x|$. The reverse triangle inequality gives $||x|-|y||\le|x-y|$, and equality holds for distinct positive inputs. Thus $L^\star=1$ and the transformed bound is tight.

exercises.title: Read a chain of weighted gains
exercises.q: Two scalar layers are $z_1=1.5x$ and $z_2=2z_1$, with output $f=z_2$. Use $X_0=9,X_1=4,X_2=1$ to check the layer inequalities $X_k(\Delta z_k)^2\le X_{k-1}(\Delta z_{k-1})^2$ and recover the total gain.
exercises.hint: Compare weighted squared increments rather than ordinary layer norms.
steps: The first layer gives $4(1.5\Delta x)^2=9(\Delta x)^2$. The second gives $(2\Delta z_1)^2=4(\Delta z_1)^2$. Both inequalities hold with equality.
Chaining them yields $|\Delta f|^2\le X_0|\Delta x|^2=9|\Delta x|^2$, so the certified gain is $3$.
The composite map is $f(x)=3x$, which attains gain $3$. Intermediate storage matrices can carry unequal coordinate scales; they are not themselves Euclidean layer Lipschitz constants.

exercises.title: Bias blindness on two reachable-pattern sets
exercises.q: Compare $f_0(x)=\operatorname{ReLU}(x)-\operatorname{ReLU}(-x)$ with $f_1(x)=\operatorname{ReLU}(x+1)-\operatorname{ReLU}(-x+1)$. Find their piecewise slopes and exact constants. What lower limit does this put on a weight-only bound shared by both?
exercises.hint: Place all kinks on the number line; the middle interval matters.
steps: For $f_0$, one neuron is active on each side of zero and $f_0(x)=x$ everywhere. Its slope is $1$ away from the kink and $L^\star(f_0)=1$.
For $f_1$, the slopes are $1$ for $x\lt-1$, $2$ for $-1\lt x\lt1$, and $1$ for $x\gt1$. The functions agree continuously at the kinks, so the maximum slope magnitude gives $L^\star(f_1)=2$.

The two networks have identical weight matrices. A bound that does not use biases must be valid for $f_1$ as well and therefore be at least $2$, even when applied to $f_0$. This is a reachability loss before any numerical optimization error.

exercises.title: PSD does not make a multiplier valid
exercises.q: Use ReLU, $v=(0,2)$, $\bar v=(-1,0)$ and $T=(e_1-e_2)(e_1-e_2)^\top$. Show that $T\succeq0$ but the coupled incremental QC is negative. Compare with $T=I$.
exercises.hint: The coupled form is $2(\Delta v_1-\Delta v_2)(\Delta z_1-\Delta z_2)-2(\Delta z_1-\Delta z_2)^2$.
steps: $T=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}=aa^\top$ with $a=(1,-1)^\top$, so $y^\top Ty=(a^\top y)^2\ge0$. It is PSD.
Here $\Delta v=(1,2)$ and $\Delta z=(0,2)$. Their channel differences are $-1$ and $-2$. The coupled form is $2(-1)(-2)-2(-2)^2=4-8=-4$, violating the proposed QC.

With $T=I$, the two scalar contributions are $2(0)(1-0)=0$ and $2(2)(2-2)=0$. Those valid constraints hold. PSD of $T$ is an algebraic property; validity of the QC for the actual activation increments is a separate requirement.

exercises.title: Check a numerical margin before trusting a status
exercises.q: Compare $M_1=\begin{bmatrix}-1&1.1\\1.1&-1\end{bmatrix}$ and $M_2=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0.9\\0.9&-1\end{bmatrix}$. Which is negative semidefinite? If the actual symmetric matrix is $M_2+E$ with a proven $\|E\|_2\le0.04$, does the certificate survive?
exercises.hint: The vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ are eigenvectors. Then bound $x^\top Ex$ by $\|E\|_2\|x\|^2$.
steps: The eigenvalues of $M_1$ are $-1+1.1=0.1$ and $-1-1.1=-2.1$. It is not negative semidefinite, regardless of a solver success flag.
$M_2$ has eigenvalues $-0.1$ and $-1.9$, so $x^\top M_2x\le-0.1\|x\|^2$ for every $x$.
The perturbation adds at most $0.04\|x\|^2$. Thus $x^\top(M_2+E)x\le-0.06\|x\|^2$, still strictly negative for nonzero $x$. A proven error bound and a margin together justify the conclusion.

exercises.title: Pooling and a hidden overlap assumption
exercises.q: A length-three signal is mapped to $y=((x_1+x_2)/2,(x_2+x_3)/2)$. Compute its Euclidean gain. Why is the non-overlapping two-point average-pooling gain $1/\sqrt2$ not valid for this map?
exercises.hint: Form the $2\times3$ pooling matrix and compute $PP^\top$.
steps: $P=\tfrac12\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}$, so $PP^\top=\tfrac14\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are $3/4$ and $1/4$.
The gain is the largest singular value, $\|P\|_2=\sqrt3/2\approx0.866025$, which exceeds $1/\sqrt2\approx0.707107$. For example $x=(1,2,1)$ attains squared ratio $4.5/6=3/4$.

The middle input is reused in both outputs. The orthogonal, disjoint windows needed for the $1/\sqrt2$ rule are absent. The general bound $1$ remains valid, but importing the tighter formula without its stride/overlap assumptions would be unsound.

exercises.title: Normalize with the correct side of an estimate
exercises.q: $W=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)$ and a power method estimates its norm as $2.5$. Compute $\|W/2.5\|_2$. Instead divide by the Frobenius upper bound $\sqrt{10}$; what norm results?
exercises.hint: The largest singular value of a positive diagonal matrix is its largest entry.
steps: The exact spectral norm is $3$. Dividing by $2.5$ gives norm $3/2.5=1.2$, so the stored layer is expansive.
The Frobenius norm is $\sqrt{3^2+1^2}=\sqrt{10}\ge3$. Dividing by it gives spectral norm $3/\sqrt{10}\approx0.948683\le1$.
A lower estimate is useful for monitoring, but a certified normalization denominator must be a proven upper bound (or the exact norm).

exercises.title: A Cayley rotation by hand
exercises.q: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}$ compute $Q=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}$ and $Q(3,-4)^\top$. Check the input and output norms.
exercises.hint: The inverse of $I+A$ is $\tfrac12\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Multiplying gives $Q=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$. Its columns are orthonormal, so $Q^\top Q=I$.
$Q(3,-4)^\top=(4,3)^\top$. Both norms are $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$.
This is a right-angle rotation. The skew-symmetric free matrix generated a norm-preserving weight by construction, without a norm penalty.

exercises.title: Forward preservation and backward preservation
exercises.q: Let $W=(1,0)^\top$. Check $W^\top W$ and $WW^\top$. Does it preserve the norm of scalar inputs? Does it preserve every output-gradient norm under $g\mapsto W^\top g$?
exercises.hint: Test the backward map on $g=(0,2)^\top$.
steps: $W^\top W=[1]$, but $WW^\top=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\ne I_2$. The matrix has orthonormal columns and lacks orthonormal rows.
For a scalar $x$, $Wx=(x,0)^\top$, so $\|Wx\|=|x|$. Forward norms are preserved.
For $g=(0,2)^\top$, $W^\top g=0$ while $\|g\|=2$. Backward preservation for every $g$ requires $WW^\top=I$, a different condition for rectangular matrices.

exercises.title: Include input preprocessing in the radius
exercises.q: A logit network has certified bound $\gamma=0.8$ in normalized coordinates. Raw inputs are normalized with coordinate standard deviations $0.5$ and $0.25$. Find a raw-input bound and the strict Euclidean radius when the raw input has margin $0.4$.
exercises.hint: The normalization matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(2,4)$; constants subtracted from inputs cancel in differences.
steps: The normalization map has spectral norm $4$. The composite raw-input logit map is therefore at most $4(0.8)=3.2$-Lipschitz.
The standard logit-margin rule gives $r=0.4/(\sqrt2\cdot3.2)=1/(8\sqrt2)\approx0.0883883$.
This certifies $\|\delta\|_2\lt r$ measured in raw input units. Using $0.8$ directly would claim a radius four times too large.

exercises.title: An analytic AOL scaling
exercises.q: For $P=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ form $T_{ii}=\sum_j|(P^\top P)_{ij}|$ and $D=T^{-1/2}$. Verify $\|PD\|_2\le1$ by computing the eigenvalues of $DP^\top PD$.
exercises.hint: The Gram matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, so the row sums are $2$ and $3$.
steps: $T=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$ and $D=\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt3)$. Thus $DP^\top PD=\begin{bmatrix}1/2&1/\sqrt6\\1/\sqrt6&2/3\end{bmatrix}$.
This symmetric matrix has trace $7/6$ and determinant $1/6$. Its eigenvalues are $1$ and $1/6$, since these have the stated sum and product.
The squared singular values of $PD$ are those eigenvalues, so $\|PD\|_2=1$. Equivalently $T-P^\top P=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}\succeq0$ gives the certificate directly.

exercises.title: A residual layer with a sharp condition
exercises.q: In scalar SLL let $W=2$, $b=0$, and $h(x)=x-2WT^{-1}\operatorname{ReLU}(W^\top x)$. Compare $T=4$ and $T=2$. Compute the piecewise slopes in each case.
exercises.hint: The sufficient condition is $T\ge W^\top W=4$.
steps: With $T=4$, the coefficient $2W/T=1$ gives $h(x)=x-\operatorname{ReLU}(2x)$. It equals $x$ on $x\le0$ and $-x$ on $x\ge0$, or $-|x|$.
The slopes are $1$ and $-1$, so the map is exactly 1-Lipschitz. The certificate condition holds at equality.
With $T=2$, $h(x)=x-2\operatorname{ReLU}(2x)$ has slopes $1$ and $-3$. Its Lipschitz constant is $3$. Invertibility and positivity of $T$ alone are insufficient; $T\ge W^\top W$ matters.

exercises.title: A scalar sandwich and its multiplier
exercises.q: Use $A=3/5$, $B=4/5$, $\Psi=2$, $b=0$, and ReLU. Find the input coefficient $U=\sqrt2\Psi^{-1}B$, output coefficient $Y=\sqrt2A\Psi$, and exact layer gain. Check $2\Lambda-Y^2-\Lambda^2U^2$ for $\Lambda=4$ and for the mistaken $\Lambda=2$.
exercises.hint: $A^2+B^2=1$. The positive scalar coefficients let you move them through ReLU.
steps: $U=2\sqrt2/5$ and $Y=6\sqrt2/5$. Thus $Y\operatorname{ReLU}(Ux)=(24/25)\operatorname{ReLU}(x)$, with exact gain $24/25=0.96$.
The correct multiplier is $\Lambda=\Psi^2=4$. Here $U^2=8/25$, $Y^2=72/25$, and $8-72/25-16(8/25)=0$. This matches the boundary identity.
For $\Lambda=2$, the same expression is $4-72/25-4(8/25)=-4/25$. The wrong multiplier fails this certificate although the layer itself remains 1-Lipschitz.

exercises.title: A finite Gramian without an infinite sum
exercises.q: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=(0,1)^\top$. Compute $X=\sum_{k=0}^\infty A^kBB^\top(A^\top)^k$. Check $X=AXA^\top+BB^\top$ and whether $X^{-1}$ exists.
exercises.hint: $A^2=0$, so only $k=0,1$ can contribute.
steps: $BB^\top=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ and $AB=(1,0)^\top$, so $ABB^\top A^\top=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$. All later terms vanish and $X=I_2$.
$AXA^\top=AA^\top=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$; adding $BB^\top$ returns $I_2=X$. This is the discrete controllability-Gramian equation.
$X$ is positive definite and invertible, with $X^{-1}=I_2$. Nilpotence makes the sum finite; controllability, visible from the independent columns $B,AB$, supplies positive definiteness.

exercises.title: Completeness depends on the certificate set
exercises.q: A direct parameterization reaches every network certified by a particular LMI at bound $1$. A network has true constant $1$ but the minimum bound from that LMI is $2$. Must the parameterization represent that network at bound $1$? Use $\operatorname{ReLU}(x)-\operatorname{ReLU}(-x)$ as the concrete case for diagonal LipSDP.
exercises.hint: Distinguish the set of truly Lipschitz networks from the subset that the LMI can certify.
steps: Completeness says that the image equals the LMI certificate set. It does not say that the certificate set equals all networks with true constant at most $1$.

The example computes $x$ and has exact constant $1$. Its weights also admit the independent all-active slope pattern, with slope $2$; diagonal LipSDP must cover that pattern and cannot return a bound below $2$.

Therefore this weight representation is outside the LipSDP certificate set at bound $1$, and completeness does not require reaching it there. The same function may have another, simpler certified representation; completeness concerns the stated weight/certificate set.

exercises.title: Coupled layers can have large ordinary norms
exercises.q: Take identity activations and weights $W_0=\operatorname{diag}(4,1/4)$, $W_1=\operatorname{diag}(1/4,4)$. Compute their norm product and the composite gain. Find $X_1$ so $W_0^\top X_1W_0=I$ and $W_1^\top W_1=X_1$.
exercises.hint: The second layer reverses the first layer's directional scaling.
steps: Both spectral norms are $4$, so their product is $16$. Yet $W_1W_0=I$, and the composite gain is exactly $1$. Identity activation is slope-restricted in $[0,1]$.
Set $X_1=\operatorname{diag}(1/16,16)$. Direct multiplication gives $W_0^\top X_1W_0=I$ and $W_1^\top W_1=X_1$.

The intermediate weighted energy is therefore equal to input energy and output energy. This example explains why coupling directions through a certificate can prove gain $1$ while enforcing ordinary norm at most $1$ for each stored layer would exclude these weights.

exercises.title: Carry a truncation factor through depth
exercises.q: For $K=\begin{bmatrix}0&-0.2\\0.2&0\end{bmatrix}$ deploy $S_2=I+K+K^2/2$ instead of $e^K$. Compute its exact norm and compare it with $1+0.2^3/6$. What bound follows for a composition of ten such layers and 1-Lipschitz activations?
exercises.hint: $K^2=-0.04I$, so $S_2=0.98I+K$ and $S_2^\top S_2$ is diagonal.
steps: The skew-exponential remainder bound is $\|e^K-S_2\|_2\le0.2^3/6=0.00133333$. Since $e^K$ is orthogonal, $\|S_2\|_2\le1.00133333$, a valid looser upper bound.

For ten layers the remainder-based product bound is $(1+0.2^3/6)^{10}\approx1.01341362$. Exact layer norms give $(\sqrt{1.0004})^{10}\approx1.00200160$. Intermediate activations can reduce the true gain, but calling the truncated network exactly 1-Lipschitz would be unjustified.

exercises.title: Contraction time and a nonzero initial storage
exercises.q: A recurrent model satisfies $\|\Delta x_t\|_P\le0.8^t\|\Delta x_0\|_P$ for equal inputs. If the initial distance is $3$, find the first integer time at which this bound is at most $0.1$. Separately, a dissipativity certificate gives $\sum_t\|\Delta y_t\|^2\le V_0+4\sum_t\|\Delta u_t\|^2$. If $V_0=4$ and input energy is $9$, what output-energy bound follows?
exercises.hint: Take logarithms carefully: $\log0.8\lt0$. For the second question keep the initial storage term.
steps: $3(0.8)^t\le0.1$ is equivalent to $t\ge\log(1/30)/\log0.8\approx15.24$, so the first integer is $16$. Indeed the bounds at $15$ and $16$ are about $0.105553$ and $0.0844425$.
The output energy is at most $4+4\cdot9=40$, giving output sequence norm at most $\sqrt{40}\approx6.32456$.

The pure incremental gain rule $\|\Delta y\|_{\ell_2}\le2\|\Delta u\|_{\ell_2}=6$ requires zero initial storage (for example equal initial states). Contraction under equal inputs and a gain statement under differing inputs answer different questions.

exercises.title: Find the equilibrium before shifting
exercises.q: For $x_{t+1}=0.5x_t+u_t$ and $u_t=0.25x_t+1$, find $(x_*,u_*)$ and the deviation dynamics. Is the origin an equilibrium of the unshifted system?
exercises.hint: Substitute the controller into the plant, then solve $x_*=x_{t+1}=x_t$.
steps: The closed loop is $x_{t+1}=0.75x_t+1$. At equilibrium $0.25x_*=1$, so $x_*=4$ and $u_*=0.25(4)+1=2$.
Set $\tilde x_t=x_t-4$. Subtracting $4=0.75(4)+1$ gives $\tilde x_{t+1}=0.75\tilde x_t$.
The origin is not an equilibrium: it moves to $1$ in one step. Stability must be studied around the actual equilibrium; subtracting the correct equilibrium removes the affine constants.

exercises.title: A Lyapunov difference is a difference of energies
exercises.q: For $x^+=0.8x$ and $V(x)=2x^2$, compute $V(x^+)-V(x)$. Evaluate $V$ before and after one step from $x=2$.
exercises.hint: Square the factor $0.8$ when substituting into $V$.
steps: $V(x^+)=2(0.8x)^2=1.28x^2$. Thus $\Delta V=(1.28-2)x^2=-0.72x^2$, strictly negative for nonzero $x$.
At $x=2$, $V=8$. The next state is $1.6$ and $V(x^+)=2(1.6)^2=5.12$, a decrease of $2.88$.
The nonnegative energy decreases and the exact trajectory is $x_t=0.8^tx_0\to0$. The negative coefficient in the Lyapunov difference certifies convergence in this scalar example.

exercises.title: An ellipsoid inside a pre-activation interval
exercises.q: For $P=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)$, describe the semi-axes of $x^\top Px\le1$. If a pre-activation is $v=2x_1+x_2$, find its maximum absolute value on this ellipsoid. Is the box $|v|\le1$ large enough?
exercises.hint: The sharp squared bound is $aP^{-1}a^\top$ for the row $a=(2,1)$.
steps: The inequality is $4x_1^2+x_2^2\le1$, with semi-axes $1/2$ and $1$. The inverse is $P^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/4,1)$.
$aP^{-1}a^\top=4(1/4)+1=2$, so $|v|\le\sqrt2$. Equality occurs at $x=P^{-1}a^\top/\sqrt2=(1/(2\sqrt2),1/\sqrt2)^\top$.
The interval $[-1,1]$ misses that attainable value. A local sector stated only there cannot be applied on the whole ellipsoid; the required half-width is at least $\sqrt2$.

exercises.title: Two shifted ReLUs need not be repeated
exercises.q: Define $\tilde\varphi_1(s)=\operatorname{ReLU}(s+1)-1$ and $\tilde\varphi_2(s)=\operatorname{ReLU}(s-1)$. Check both values at $s=0$ and $s=1/2$. Are these the same scalar function?
exercises.hint: Both shifts remove the value at the basepoint, but the basepoints lie on different sides of the kink.
steps: At $s=0$, the values are $1-1=0$ and $\operatorname{ReLU}(-1)=0$. Both shifted maps vanish at the origin.
At $s=1/2$, the first value is $1.5-1=0.5$, whereas the second is $\operatorname{ReLU}(-0.5)=0$. Hence the maps differ.
Each remains slope-restricted in $[0,1]$. Individual sector/slope QCs survive the shift, but an argument that assumes one identical repeated function across these two channels does not.

exercises.title: A sector bound and a slope bound differ
exercises.q: For tanh on $[-1,1]$, compute the centred lower sector bound $\alpha=\tanh(1)$ and lower slope bound $\mu=1-\tanh^2(1)$. Evaluate the $[0,1]$ sector form at $v=1,w=\tanh(1)$. Why does substituting $\mu$ for $\alpha$ lose information?
exercises.hint: A sector compares a point with the fixed equilibrium; a slope bound compares any two points.
steps: $\alpha\approx0.76159416$ is the smallest chord slope from the origin on this interval. The smallest derivative is $\mu\approx0.41997434$, attained at the endpoints.
The global $[0,1]$ QC is $2w(v-w)$. Substitution gives $2\tanh(1)(1-\tanh(1))\approx0.363137\ge0$.

The slope bound implies the weaker sector $[\mu,1]$, but its smaller lower endpoint admits more nonlinearities. The larger centred chord bound $\alpha$ is legitimate for the fixed equilibrium and can improve the local stability certificate.

exercises.title: Propagate an affine interval with signed weights
exercises.q: A hidden-output box has centre $c=(1,-1)$ and radius vector $r=(0.2,0.5)$. The next pre-activation is $v=2w_1-3w_2+1$. Find its exact interval over this box and the corner attaining the upper endpoint.
exercises.hint: The centre is $ac+b$ and the radius is $|a|r$.
steps: To maximize $v$, take $w_1=1.2$ because its coefficient is positive and $w_2=-1.5$ because its coefficient is negative. This gives $2.4+4.5+1=7.9$.
This endpoint is exact over the independent-coordinate box. If the true hidden outputs are correlated, that corner may be unreachable; the interval remains sound but may be conservative.

exercises.title: Why an unstable plant needs a local lower sector
exercises.q: Consider $x^+=1.2x-0.5w$ and the uncertainty family $w=dx$ for $d\in[\alpha,1]$, $0\le\alpha\le1$. Find when every member is asymptotically stable. Compare $\alpha=0$ and $\alpha=0.5$.
exercises.hint: The scalar multiplier $1.2-0.5d$ must lie strictly between $-1$ and $1$.
steps: The multiplier decreases with $d$ and ranges from $0.7$ to $1.2-0.5\alpha$. Its smallest value is already positive and below one.
Uniform strict stability therefore requires $1.2-0.5\alpha\lt1$, or $\alpha\gt0.4$. At $\alpha=0.4$ the endpoint has multiplier one, so asymptotic stability fails.

For $\alpha=0$ the family includes $d=0$, the unstable open loop with multiplier $1.2$. For $\alpha=0.5$, all multipliers lie in $[0.7,0.95]$. A valid local sector can exclude a controller that is effectively switched off.

exercises.title: A hard IQC can have a negative time sample
exercises.q: Let $w_t=v_t/2$, $a_t=v_t-w_t$, $b_t=w_t$, with $a_{-1}=0$ and $(v_0,v_1)=(2,1)$. Evaluate $b_t(a_t-a_{t-1})$ at both times and its partial sums. Show why nonnegative sums are possible without nonnegative individual terms.
steps: $a_0=b_0=1$ and $a_1=b_1=1/2$. The terms are $1(1-0)=1$ and $(1/2)(1/2-1)=-1/4$. Their partial sums are $1$ and $3/4$.
For any finite sequence, summing the identity in the hint gives $\sum_{t=0}^N a_t(a_t-a_{t-1})=\tfrac12a_N^2+\tfrac12\sum_{t=0}^N(a_t-a_{t-1})^2\ge0$. The initial square vanishes because $a_{-1}=0$.
This is a finite-horizon, or hard, IQC for this relation. A Lyapunov proof may use its summed nonnegativity; deleting a negative sample as though the IQC held pointwise would change the argument.

exercises.title: Close the local-sector invariance argument
exercises.q: A scalar map is $x^+=x/2$ for $|x|\le1$ and $x^+=2x$ for $|x|\gt1$. With $V=x^2$ prove that $\{V\le1\}$ is invariant and contained in the ROA of zero. Does the same local calculation prove convergence from $x_0=1.1$?
exercises.hint: Use the local rule at the current state, then prove the next state remains in its domain.
steps: If $V(x_t)\le1$, then $|x_t|\le1$, so the local rule applies and $V(x_{t+1})=V(x_t)/4\le1/4\le1$. This proves invariance by induction from any initial state in the set.
Induction also gives $V(x_t)=4^{-t}V(x_0)$, hence $x_t\to0$. Thus the entire sublevel set is in the ROA, using only the rule valid there.

At $x_0=1.1$ the exterior rule applies and $x_t=1.1\,2^t$, which diverges. A certificate based on local constraints needs the containment/invariance step; its conclusion extends only over the certified initial-state set.

exercises.title: Check a stability LMI entirely by hand
exercises.q: For $x^+=1.2x-0.5w$ and the sector $w/x\in[0.5,1]$, use $V=x^2$ and multiplier $T=1$. Expand $\Delta V+2(w-0.5x)(x-w)$ as a quadratic form. Prove its matrix is negative definite and explain the stability conclusion when the sector is local.
exercises.hint: For a symmetric $2\times2$ matrix, a negative first diagonal entry and positive determinant imply negative definiteness.
steps: The Lyapunov difference is $0.44x^2-1.2xw+0.25w^2$. The QC is $-x^2+3xw-2w^2$. Their sum is $-0.56x^2+1.8xw-1.75w^2$.

The matrix is $M=\begin{bmatrix}-0.56&0.9\\0.9&-1.75\end{bmatrix}$. Its determinant is $0.98-0.81=0.17\gt0$ and its first diagonal is negative, so $M\prec0$ (eigenvalues approximately $-2.23390,-0.0761001$).

On the sector, the QC is nonnegative, so $\Delta V\le\Delta V+\mathrm{QC}\lt0$ away from zero. For a local sector, one must also exhibit a sublevel set contained in its pre-activation domain and use invariance; the LMI alone does not supply a global conclusion.

exercises.title: A disturbance changes convergence into a bound
exercises.q: Suppose $V(x)=\|x\|_2^2$ and a closed-loop certificate proves $V_{t+1}\le0.5V_t+2d_t^2$ with $|d_t|\le0.1$. Starting with $V_0\le0.25$, derive a finite-time bound, prove invariance of $V\le0.25$, and state the limiting state-radius bound.
exercises.hint: Unroll the recursion and sum a geometric series. A persistent disturbance need not vanish.
steps: The disturbance term is at most $0.02$. Recursion gives $V_t\le0.5^tV_0+0.02\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}0.5^j=0.5^tV_0+0.04(1-0.5^t)$.
If $V_t\le0.25$, then $V_{t+1}\le0.125+0.02=0.145\le0.25$. Hence the sublevel set is invariant for every allowed disturbance sequence.
Taking a limit superior gives $\limsup_tV_t\le0.04$, so $\limsup_t\|x_t\|_2\le0.2$. This proves a disturbance-dependent ultimate bound, not convergence to zero under arbitrary persistent disturbance.

exercises.title: Audit three tempting certificate shortcuts
exercises.q: A reviewer proposes: (i) couple all shifted ReLU channels with equilibrium pre-activations $(0,0,1)$ as one repeated nonlinearity; (ii) treat every time sample of a hard IQC as nonnegative; (iii) reuse a fixed-network stability certificate after a small unbounded-in-the-proof weight update. For each proposal identify the missing justification and a valid repair.
exercises.hint: Check which functions are identical, what time quantifier an IQC has, and which matrices the certificate actually covers.
steps: (i) Channels 1 and 2 have the identical shifted map $\operatorname{ReLU}(s)$; channel 3 has $\operatorname{ReLU}(s+1)-1$. At $s=-1/2$ their values are $0$ and $-1/2$. Coupling justified by repetition may be used within the equal-shift group, or replaced by per-channel diagonal constraints across all three.

(ii) A hard IQC guarantees each finite-horizon sum is nonnegative. Individual terms may be negative. Sum the dissipation inequality with the IQC, retaining its filter state and initial-state assumptions, instead of asserting pointwise nonnegativity.

(iii) The changed weights change the LMI and possibly local bounds/equilibria. Recompute and recheck the certificate, or establish a perturbation bound smaller than a proven feasibility margin. A small numerical update alone does not prove that the old certificate applies.

exercises.title: Turn a label claim into a scalar specification
exercises.q: On $x\in[0,1]$, logits are $f_1(x)=2x+1$ and $f_2(x)=-x+2$. Write the specification for class 1 to beat class 2, find its worst case, and give a counterexample. If an incomplete verifier returns upper bound $1.4$, does that number alone prove failure?
exercises.hint: The scalar violation objective is $f_2-f_1$, not $f_1-f_2$.
steps: The violation is $p(x)=f_2(x)-f_1(x)=1-3x$, which is largest at $x=0$, with $p^\star=1$. Thus the desired property fails.
The input $x=0$ is an explicit counterexample: the logits are $(1,2)$ and class 2 wins.

An upper bound $\bar p=1.4\gt0$ by itself says only that the relaxation did not verify the property. Here failure is established by the actual input and its forward evaluation, not by the positive upper bound.

exercises.title: One affine interval and one ReLU
exercises.q: For $x_1\in[1,2]$, $x_2\in[-1,1]$, find the exact interval for $z=2x_1-3x_2+1$ and its ReLU output. Give input corners attaining the two endpoints.
exercises.hint: Positive coefficients maximize at the upper input endpoint; negative coefficients maximize at the lower endpoint.
steps: The minimum is $2(1)-3(1)+1=0$, attained at $(1,1)$. The maximum is $2(2)-3(-1)+1=8$, attained at $(2,-1)$. Hence $z\in[0,8]$.
ReLU is monotone, so its output interval is $[\operatorname{ReLU}(0),\operatorname{ReLU}(8)]=[0,8]$. This neuron is stable active, including its zero boundary.
In centre-radius form the input centre is $(1.5,0)$ and radius $(0.5,1)$; the pre-activation centre is $4$ and radius $2(0.5)+3(1)=4$, giving the same result.

exercises.title: An unstable ReLU triangle
exercises.q: On $z\in[-2,3]$ write the chord upper bound and choose lower line $h_L(z)=0.4z$. Check both inequalities at $z=-1$ and $z=1$. Why is a negative lower-line value allowed?
exercises.hint: The chord joins $(-2,0)$ to $(3,3)$. A lower bound need not be an attainable activation value.
steps: The chord is $h_U(z)=\frac35(z+2)$. At $z=-1$, $h_L=-0.4\le0=\operatorname{ReLU}(-1)\le0.6=h_U$.
At $z=1$, $h_L=0.4\le1\le1.8=h_U$. More generally, $0\le0.4\le1$ makes $0.4z$ a valid ReLU lower line across the entire interval.
A relaxation encloses the true graph and may include artificial points. A negative lower value is conservative, while a lower value above the actual ReLU would be unsound.

exercises.title: Choose the conformal order statistic
exercises.q: Nine calibration scores sorted increasingly are $0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.9$. At miscoverage level $\alpha=0.2$, compute the split-conformal index and threshold. For absolute-error scores and prediction $\hat y=2$, write the prediction interval.
exercises.hint: Use $k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$, with $n+1$, not $n$.
steps: $k=\lceil10(0.8)\rceil=8$, so the threshold is the eighth calibration score, $\hat q=0.8$.
The set $|y-2|\le0.8$ is the interval $[1.2,2.8]$. The endpoints are included because the conformal set uses $\le$.

With a score fixed before calibration and exchangeable calibration/test examples, the marginal coverage is at least $0.8$. The theorem averages over calibration and test randomness; it is not a guarantee at each individual input.

exercises.title: Interval independence can invent an impossible output
exercises.q: For $x\in[-1,1]$, let $a_1=\operatorname{ReLU}(x)$, $a_2=\operatorname{ReLU}(x)$, $f=a_1-a_2$. Compute the IBP output interval and the exact output set. What information did IBP discard?
exercises.hint: The two activation intervals are identical, but their values cannot be chosen independently.
steps: Each hidden interval is $[0,1]$. Treating them as independent gives $f\in[0-1,1-0]=[-1,1]$.
The exact network always has $a_1=a_2$, so $f(x)=0$ and the exact output set is $\{0\}$.

IBP kept coordinate ranges and forgot equality between the coordinates. It remains sound because $\{0\}\subset[-1,1]$. A relaxation preserving this equality, or algebraic cancellation before bounding, recovers the tighter result.

exercises.title: Select a CROWN line by the output sign
exercises.q: Let $f(z)=1-2\operatorname{ReLU}(z)$ on $[-1,2]$, with upper chord $h_U(z)=\frac23(z+1)$ and lower line $h_L=0$. Which line gives an upper bound on $f$, and which a lower bound? Show at $z=-1/2$ why using $1-2h_U$ as an upper bound fails.
exercises.hint: Multiplying an activation inequality by $-2$ reverses its direction.
steps: From $h_L\le\operatorname{ReLU}(z)\le h_U$ we get $1-2h_U\le f(z)\le1-2h_L=1$. Thus the lower activation line supplies the upper output bound.
The lower output line is $1-\frac43(z+1)$, whose minimum on the interval is $-3$ at $z=2$. The exact function ranges from $-3$ to $1$, so both final scalar bounds are tight here.
At $z=-1/2$, the actual output is $1$, while $1-2h_U=1-2(1/3)=1/3$. It cannot be an upper bound on a value equal to $1$; it is a valid lower bound.

exercises.title: A smoothing radius and its confidence statement
exercises.q: An independent Monte-Carlo confidence procedure returns $\underline p_A=\Phi(2)\approx0.977249868$ at confidence $99.9\%$, with Gaussian noise scale $\sigma=0.5$. Compute the certified Euclidean radius and a sufficient infinity-norm radius in dimension $100$. What happens if the lower bound is instead $0.5$?
exercises.hint: The single-probability rule is $R=\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\underline p_A)$.
steps: Because $\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(2))=2$, the Euclidean radius is $R=0.5(2)=1$. On the confidence event, the ideal smoothed classifier keeps label $A$ for all perturbations with Euclidean norm strictly below $1$.
$\|\delta\|_2\le\sqrt{100}\|\delta\|_\infty=10\|\delta\|_\infty$, so a sufficient strict infinity-norm radius is $0.1$.

The confidence is over the probability-estimation samples, and the certified object is the smoothed classifier. If $\underline p_A=0.5$, the rule produces zero radius and CERTIFY abstains; it does not supply a positive-radius certificate.

exercises.title: Validation needs a sampling margin
exercises.q: A fixed controller is evaluated on fresh i.i.d. trials with a success indicator in $[0,1]$. At one-sided confidence $99\%$ and tolerance $t=0.1$, compute the sufficient Hoeffding sample size. If the observed success fraction is $0.98$, what population success lower bound follows? Can this tolerance certify target success $0.95$?
exercises.hint: Use $M\ge\ln(1/\alpha)/(2t^2)$ and subtract $t$ from the observed fraction.
steps: Here $\alpha=0.01$, so $M\ge\ln100/0.02\approx230.25851$. The integer sample count is at least $231$.
With probability at least $0.99$, the population success probability is at least $\hat\phi-t=0.98-0.1=0.88$. The observed fraction itself is not the population guarantee.

To certify population success $0.95$ with this tolerance would require $\hat\phi\ge1.05$, which is impossible. Reduce $t$ and increase the sample size; keep validation independent of controller selection or account for selection explicitly.

exercises.title: The same affine bound over different input balls
exercises.q: A backward relaxation yields the exact affine expression $g(x)=3x_1-4x_2+2$. Around $x_0=(1,2)$ with radius $\varepsilon=0.2$, compute its ranges for Euclidean and infinity-norm input balls, and give perturbations attaining the lower endpoints. Explain why the radii cannot be exchanged unchanged.
exercises.hint: The dual norms of the coefficient row $(3,-4)$ are $5$ for an $\ell_2$ ball and $7$ for an $\ell_\infty$ ball.
steps: The centre value is $3-8+2=-3$. On the Euclidean ball, the deviation is bounded by $0.2\sqrt{3^2+(-4)^2}=1$, so the exact range is $[-4,-2]$. The lower endpoint is attained by $\delta=-0.2(3,-4)/5=(-0.12,0.16)$.
On the infinity-norm ball, the deviation is $0.2(|3|+|-4|)=1.4$, giving $[-4.4,-1.6]$. The minimizing perturbation is $\delta=(-0.2,0.2)$, choosing the sign against each coefficient.

The infinity-norm ball with the same numerical radius contains vectors with larger Euclidean norm. The correct dual norm is part of the specification; reusing the Euclidean bound unchanged on that larger set would miss attainable values.

exercises.title: A trajectory budget and finite calibration resolution
exercises.q: For four future times you want total miscoverage at most $0.1$. Allocate equal per-time budgets and compute the conformal order index for $n=39$ and for $n=19$ calibration trajectories. Would using $90\%$ marginal coverage at every time alone imply $90\%$ joint coverage?
exercises.hint: Use a union bound, then compare $k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$ with $n$.
steps: Choose per-time miscoverage $\alpha=0.1/4=0.025$. Then the union bound gives joint coverage at least $1-4(0.025)=0.9$ without requiring independence between times.

For $n=39$, $k=\lceil40(0.975)\rceil=39$, so the threshold is the largest observed score. For $n=19$, $k=\lceil20(0.975)\rceil=20\gt19$, so the valid threshold is $+\infty$; the data cannot supply a finite threshold at this nominal resolution.

Four marginal $90\%$ statements give only the union-bound lower bound $1-4(0.1)=0.6$. Even independent $90\%$ coverage events would have joint probability $0.9^4=0.6561$, not $0.9$. A horizon guarantee needs its own budget and the exchangeability assumptions.

exercises.title: Compare an exact scenario tail with an explicit bound
exercises.q: A scenario program meets the theorem assumptions with $d=3$, target violation $\varepsilon=0.1$ and design failure probability $\beta=0.05$. Compute the explicit sufficient integer count from $N\ge\frac2\varepsilon(\ln(1/\beta)+d)$. Check the exact binomial tail at $N=60$ and $61$. State what probability is bounded.
exercises.hint: For $d=3$, sum the binomial probabilities for $i=0,1,2$. The outer randomness is the design sample.
steps: The explicit rule gives $N\ge20(\ln20+3)\approx119.91465$, so $N=120$ suffices.

The exact tail is $S_N=0.9^N+N(0.1)0.9^{N-1}+\binom N2(0.1)^2 0.9^{N-2}$. It gives $S_{60}\approx0.05304508\gt0.05$ and $S_{61}\approx0.04911828\le0.05$. The tail decreases with $N$, so $61$ is the smallest admissible count.

The theorem states that, with probability at least $0.95$ over the sampled design constraints, the returned solution has population violation probability at most $0.1$. It does not prove zero violation for every uncertainty realization; convexity, feasibility/solution assumptions and matching i.i.d. deployment sampling remain necessary.

exercises.title: Conditioning on planner feasibility changes the bound
exercises.q: A conformal planning argument proves $\mathbb P(\text{feasible and unsafe})\le0.04$, while $\mathbb P(\text{feasible})=0.5$. What upper bound follows on failure conditional on feasibility? Does the argument prove unconditional safety at least $0.96$ if behavior on infeasible runs is unspecified?
exercises.hint: Use the definition of conditional probability; the event inclusion controls only one part of all runs.
steps: $\mathbb P(\text{unsafe}\mid\text{feasible})=\mathbb P(\text{unsafe and feasible})/0.5\le0.04/0.5=0.08$. Thus the conditional safety lower bound from these facts is $0.92$.

Infeasible runs have probability $0.5$ and may all be unsafe. The given facts alone therefore permit unconditional unsafe probability as high as $0.5+0.04=0.54$, yielding only the lower bound $0.46$ on safety.

To obtain the intended unconditional safety statement, prove almost-sure feasibility or add a certified safe fallback for infeasible cases. Simply discarding infeasible runs changes the probability space and does not preserve the original $0.96$ claim.
